newsitem.title: USA: Dow open seen steady to higher as rally steams on.
newsitem.headline: Dow open seen steady to higher as rally steams on.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to start steady to higher a day after piercing the 6500 level for the first time ever.

While analysts had expected some profit-taking to emerge during Monday's session, the Dow plowed ahead by more than 76 points to its 12th record close this month, leaving few on Wall Street willing to stand in the way of the current run.
"It's just unrelenting," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities. "It's very difficult to make the call that suddenly it's going to stop."

Despite repeated predictions in recent weeks that the market would pause for breath, stocks have instead gained momentum over the course of their climb, pushing the Dow to 500 points in gains in little more than three weeks.

"What we're seeing here is basically what we saw in IBM last week," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "There is a rotation going on in the blue chip index and until the rotation is exhausted we're going to see the market move higher."
For now, skeptics have taken to the sidelines, reluctant to fight the rally during its strongest phase.
But analysts remain convinced that at some point, the market will have to correct the sharp gains of the last month.
"One of these days this market is going to turn around," Cardillo said. "It's going to be swift but one where we could lose five percent."
Investors will receive several indicators today about a key sector of the economy at this time of year: retail.

Weekly BTM-Schroders and Redbook retail sales data are due today and could provide a glimpse into the Christmas shopping season outlook. Also, at 1000 EST/1500 GMT, the Conference Board will release its November consumer confidence survey.
Investors in retail chains would obviously welcome a strong set of reports, but the overall market is a different story, Wachtel said.
"The market loves moderation and one thing that would threaten this market would be a very strong Christmas," he said. "But we're not going to have a very strong Christmas."
In London, the FTSE 100 climbed 24 points to 4079. U.S. stocks traded flat in London, however, as investors grew wary of Wall Street's recent run of records.
In Tokyo, stocks finished higher ahead of release of the "Tankan" business survey. The Nikkei-225 rose 125 to 21,418.
U.S. Treasuries were moderately higher. The benchmark 30-year bond rose 8/32, to yield 6.41 percent.
The dollar edged lower in Japan but held above the 112 yen level. The greenback stood firm in Europe, rising to just shy of 21-month highs against the Swiss Franc.
The December S&P 500 future rose 1.2 points to 761.15.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column reports that some value investors are selling positions in Applied Materials Inc after a 50 percent run-up in the shares. Taking the place of value investors are momentum players, the column adds.

The New York Times Marketplace column explores why a customer statement from Everen Securities showed the firm was still employing trading practices outlawed last year. Everen said it will modify the statement, which was erroneous, the Times reports.
-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730
